title: Murray's Witch-Cult in Western Europe: Influential but Discredited Thesis
description: Margaret Murray, an Egyptologist at University College London, published The Witch-Cult in Western Europe in 1921, arguing that the women and men executed as witches were actually practitioners of a genuine pre-Christian fertility religion organized in covens of thirteen — a religion systematically persecuted by the Christian church. Murray used published witch trial confessions selectively, ignoring the torture context and contradictory evidence, to construct her 'Dianic cult' thesis. Despite being rejected by professional medievalists and historians almost immediately, Murray's thesis became enormously influential in popular culture, was adopted by Gerald Gardner to found modern Wicca, and shaped public understanding of the witch trials for decades.
historiographical_note: Norman Cohn's Europe's Inner Demons (1975) and Keith Thomas's Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) both explicitly refuted Murray's thesis. Ronald Hutton's The Triumph of the Moon (1999) provided the definitive scholarly demolition while tracing the cultural channels through which Murray's ideas reached popular consciousness. The Murray thesis is a case study in how a discredited scholarly idea can persist and proliferate in popular culture independently of academic correction.
source_method: Murray, The Witch-Cult in Western Europe (1921); Hutton, The Triumph of the Moon (1999); Cohn, Europe's Inner Demons (1975)
